A. P. J. Abdul Kalam: Born and raised in a Muslim family in Rameswaram, Tamil Nadu, Kalam studied physics and aerospace engineering.

Empire of Japan: The South Seas Mandate and concessions such as the Kwantung Leased Territory were de jure not internal parts of the empire but dependent territories.

Polish People's Party: Waldemar Pawlak. The Polish People's Party (Polish: Polskie Stronnictwo Ludowe, PSL) is a conservative political party in Poland.
National People's Party (India): P. A. Sangma. Sangma after his expulsion from the Nationalist Congress Party in July 2012, it was accorded national party status on 7 June 2019.
Judea: Israel. The name is derived from the Hebrew name Yehudah, and was used during the Babylonian, Persian, Hellenistic, and Roman periods.
In which country is the Radical Civic Union based?
Radical Civic Union: Argentina. The Radical Civic Union (Spanish: Unión Cívica Radical, UCR) is a major political party in Argentina.
In which country is Battle of Tannenberg?
Battle of Tannenberg: Poland. The outcome brought considerable prestige to the German army commander, General Paul von Hindenburg, and his rising staff officer, General Erich Ludendorff.
Alans: Pryazovia. Modern historians have connected the Alans with the Central Asian Yancai of Chinese sources and with the Aorsi of Roman sources.
In which country is Battle of Kadesh?
Battle of Kadesh: Syria. At the Orontes River, the armies engaged each other just upstream of Lake Homs and near the stronghold of Kadesh, along what is today the Lebanon–Syria border.
In which country is Somali Civil War?
Somali Civil War: Somalia. It grew out of resistance to the military junta which was led by Siad Barre during the 1980s.
Belgae: Gaul. The Roman province of Gallia Belgica was named after the continental Belgae.
In which country is Battle of Waterloo?
Battle of Waterloo: United Kingdom of the Netherlands. The French Imperial Army under the command of Napoleon I was defeated by two armies of the Seventh Coalition.
In which country was Grand Duchy of Finland?
Grand Duchy of Finland: Russian Empire. It existed from 1809 to 1917 as an autonomous state within the Russian Empire.
In which country was East India Company based?

East India Company: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. The East India Company (EIC) was an English, and later British, joint-stock company that was founded in 1600 and dissolved in 1874.
Which of these is an official language of Paris Commune?
Paris Commune: French. During the Franco-Prussian War of 1870–1871, the French National Guard had defended Paris, and working class radicalism grew among its soldiers.
Which of these was an official language of Roman Kingdom?
Roman Kingdom: Latin. Little is certain about the kingdom's history as no records and few inscriptions from the time of the kings have survived.
Which of these is an official language of OECD?
OECD: English. It was founded in 1961 to stimulate economic progress and world trade.
Of which country is Kharkiv the capital?
Kharkiv is the capital of Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic. The first iterations of the Ukrainian SSR were established during the Russian Revolution, particularly after the Bolshevik Revolution.

This militant leader, who took office in November 2022 and died the following April, served as the fourth so-called caliph of the Islamic State and was reportedly the first Syrian to hold that role. Who was he?
Abu al-Hussein al-Husseini al-Qurashi (died 29 April 2023) was the fourth caliph of the Islamic State and allegedly the first Syrian to serve as caliph.
A polar explorer turned admiral, he declared himself 'Supreme Ruler of Russia' in 1918 and led a White military dictatorship during the Civil War — who is it?
Alexander Kolchak was Russian admiral and White movement leader (1874–1920).
She earned a doctorate in quantum chemistry in East Germany before politics, then became the first woman — and first East German — to lead her country as Chancellor. Who is she?
Angela Merkel (ne Kasner; born 17 July 1954) is a German stateswoman and retired politician who served as Chancellor of Germany from 2005 to 2021.

Founded in 1891 and now Australia's oldest active political movement, this centre-left force has governed federally since the 2022 election and rules five of the country's eight states and territories — which political movement?
Australian Labor Party (ALP) is the major social democratic political party in Australia.
Once Lord Mayor of Dublin, this Fianna Fáil leader became the second-longest-serving Taoiseach before resigning in 2008 amid the Mahon Tribunal's revelations — who is he?
Bertie Ahern (born 12 September 1951) is an Irish former Fianna Fil politician who served as Taoiseach from 1997 to 2008, and as Leader of Fianna Fil from 1994 to 2008.
Strongest in the 1830s and revived after Spain's defeat in 1898, this traditionalist movement repeatedly clashed with liberalism in a string of civil wars — what movement is it?

Carlism is a traditionalist and legitimist political movement in Spain aimed at establishing an alternative branch of the Bourbon dynasty, one descended from Don Carlos, Count of Molina (1788-1855), on the Spanish throne.

A fierce 1930s champion of fighter aircraft when the U.S. Army favored high-altitude bombing, this American aviator retired in 1937 to advise China — then led the legendary 'Flying Tigers.' Who was he?
Claire Lee Chennault (September 6, 1893 - July 27, 1958) was an American military aviator best known for his leadership of the "Flying Tigers" and the Chinese Nationalist Air Force in World War II.
In 1618, disgruntled Protestant nobles threw two royal governors and their secretary from a Bohemian castle window, coining an English word for this dramatic form of ejection — what's the term?
End of World War II in Europe
Defenestrations of Prague were three incidents in the history of Bohemia in which people were defenestrated (thrown out of a window).
This Indian politician served as Maharashtra's 20th chief minister before later becoming deputy chief minister, all while chairing a major regional political party since 2023 — who is he?
Eknath Shinde (born 9 February 1964) is an Indian politician who has served as the 10th Deputy Chief Minister of Maharashtra alongside Sunetra Pawar under Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis.

This far-right, authoritarian political ideology rose to prominence in early-20th-century Europe and is characterized by support for a dictatorial leader, centralized autocracy, and forcible suppression of opposition — what is this ideology called?
Fascism is a far-right, authoritarian, and ultranationalist political ideology and movement that rose to prominence in early-20th-century Europe.
Before becoming governor of California, this Democrat was mayor of San Francisco and founded the PlumpJack winery with Gordon Getty as an investor. Who is he?
Gavin Newsom (born October 10, 1967) is an American politician and businessman serving as the governor of California since 2019.
Never renouncing her father's ideology, this woman worked for a West German intelligence agency in the 1960s while remaining closely tied to neo-Nazi circles — who was she?
Gudrun Burwitz (ne Himmler; 8 August 1929 - 24 May 2018) was the daughter of Heinrich Himmler and Margarete Himmler.
This king consort of Scotland married Mary, Queen of Scots in 1565 and was killed less than two years after the birth of their son — who was he?
Henry Stuart, Lord Darnley (1546 - 10 February 1567) was King of Scotland as the second husband of Mary, Queen of Scots, from 29 July 1565 until his murder.

This nomadic people swept out of Central Asia into Eastern Europe between the 4th and 6th centuries CE, pushing Goths and Alans westward and building a vast but short-lived empire on Rome's Danube frontier — who were they?

Huns were a nomadic people who lived in Central Asia, the Caucasus, and Eastern Europe between the 4th and 6th centuries CE. By 370 CE, the Huns had arrived on the Volga, causing the westwards movement of Goths and Alans.
This mid-1740s bid to restore the exiled Stuarts to the British throne began in the Scottish Highlands and ended when its army turned back from Derby in December — which rebellion?
Jacobite rising of 1745 was an attempt to regain the British throne for the exiled House of Stuart.
A well-traveled businessman who offered his villa for the secret 1933 meetings that made Hitler chancellor, he rose to become Nazi Germany's foreign minister — who was he?
Joachim von Ribbentrop (30 April 1893 - 16 October 1946) was a German politician, diplomat, and war criminal who served as Minister of Foreign Affairs of Nazi Germany from 1938 to 1945.
A mountain range on Pluto and an asteroid both bear her name — fitting for the Japanese climber who was the first woman atop Everest and the first to bag the Seven Summits. Who was she?
Junko Tabei (ne Ishibashi; 22 September 1939 - 20 October 2016) was a Japanese mountaineer, author and teacher.
Carved out of a former Electorate after Napoleon dissolved the Holy Roman Empire in 1806, this southern German monarchy lasted until 1918 — which one?
Kingdom of Württemberg was a German state that existed from 1806 to 1918, occupying territory in what is now the southern German federal state of Baden-Wrttemberg.

Born from the anti-authoritarian faction that split from the Marxists within the International Workingmen's Association, this political tradition champions workers' self-management while rejecting the state — what is it called?
Libertarian socialism is an anti-authoritarian and anti-capitalist political current that emphasises self-governance and workers' self-management.
A leading Indian LGBT activist who runs the Lakshya Trust, he is the probable heir to a former Maharaja and the world's first openly gay prince — who is it?
Manvendra Singh Gohil (born 23 September 1965) is a son and probable heir of former Maharaja of Rajpipla.

Before founding Herut and Likud and becoming an Israeli prime minister, he led the militant Irgun and proclaimed a 1944 revolt against British rule, behind attacks like the King David Hotel bombing — who was he?
Menachem Begin (16 August 1913 - 9 March 1992) was an Israeli politician who founded Herut and Likud and served as prime minister of Israel from 1977 to 1983.
Serving as the sixth chief of a major right-wing Hindu nationalist organization since 2009, this Indian activist was born in 1950 — who is he?

Mohan Bhagwat (born 11 September 1950) is an Indian activist who is serving as the sixth and current Sarsanghchalak (Chief) of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), a right-wing Hindutva paramilitary organisation, since 2009.
Founded in 2020 by a cosmetics-company magnate, this liberal-leaning party takes a moderately supportive stance toward Vladimir Putin while opposing much of the ruling party's agenda — which party?
New People (Russia) is a political party in Russia formed in 2020.
President Obama declared this 13-year U.S. military campaign against al-Qaeda and the Taliban officially over on 28 December 2014 — what was its codename?
Operation Enduring Freedom (OEF) was the official name used by the U.S.

This form of altruism is defined as private initiatives aimed at the public good and quality of life, often used interchangeably with 'charity,' a practice traced back to ancient Egypt — what's the term?
Philanthropy is a form of altruism that consists of "private initiatives for the public good, focusing on quality of life".
He led the Indian National Congress as president from 2017 to 2019, then went on to become the 12th Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha — which scion of a famous political family?
Rahul Gandhi (born 19 June 1970) is an Indian politician.

Rising to major general by 1979, this South Korean army officer backed his military academy friend's coup that year and later became, in 1987, the first president chosen by direct popular vote. Who is he?
Roh Tae-woo (4 December 1932 - 26 October 2021) was a South Korean army general and politician who served as the sixth president of South Korea from 1988 to 1993.
This confederation of ancient Iranian horse-riding nomadic peoples dominated the Pontic steppe from around the 5th century BC to the 4th century AD — name the people?
Sarmatians (Ancient) were a large confederation of ancient Iranian equestrian nomadic peoples who dominated the Pontic steppe from around the 5th century BC to the 4th century AD.
Once one of the largest states in African history, this Sahelian power made Gao its capital under Sonni Ali and later controlled the trade hubs of Timbuktu and Djenné — which state?
Songhai Empire was a state located in the western part of the Sahel during the 15th and 16th centuries.
Descended from Shem's line through Arpachshad, this Genesis patriarch fathered Abraham and appears in genealogies from Chronicles to the Gospel of Luke. Who is he?
Terah was a biblical figure in the Book of Genesis.
Head of state for nearly 26 years and dominant in his nation's politics for 31, this Finnish president was so unopposed in later elections that historians often call him an autocrat — who was he?
Urho Kekkonen (3 September 1900 - 31 August 1986), often referred to by his initials UKK, was a Finnish politician who served as the eighth and longest-serving president of Finland from 1956 to 1982.

He bought a small Ohio newspaper, The Marion Star, and built it up before riding into the Senate and then the White House in 1921 — beloved at his death in 1923, until the scandals surfaced. Which president?
Warren G. Harding (November 2, 1865 - August 2, 1923) was the 29th president of the United States, serving from 1921 until his death in 1923.
This Israeli military officer commanded an elite unit during the daring 1976 raid that freed hostages held by hijackers at a Ugandan airport — who was he?
Yonatan Netanyahu (March 13, 1946 - July 4, 1976) was an Israeli military officer who commanded Sayeret Matkal during the Entebbe raid.
The first Ottoman sultan to travel diplomatically to Western Europe — visiting Paris, London, and Vienna in 1867 — he was overthrown in a coup in 1876. Who was he?
Abdulaziz: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1861 to 1876.
Son of King Telamon, this towering Greek warrior was considered second only to Achilles in Homer's Iliad — who is he?
Ajax the Great: Character in Greek Mythology.

Alfonso VI of León and Castile

Alfonso VI of León and Castile

On Interpol's top-10 most-wanted list for robberies in the 1970s and '80s, this Serbian warlord later led the feared Serb Volunteer Guard through the Yugoslav Wars — by what single name was he known?
Arkan: Serbian paramilitary commander and mobster (1952–2000)
Introduced to Marxism while imprisoned, he founded the Parcham faction of Afghanistan's communist party and led the country as its general secretary through the early 1980s. Who was he?
Also known as Hipponous, this Greek hero tamed the winged horse Pegasus and slew the fire-breathing Chimera — who is he?
Serving as Russia's de facto regent before becoming tsar in 1598 after the death of the last Rurik dynasty ruler, this leader's reign preceded the chaotic Time of Troubles — who is he?
Boris Godunov: Tsar of Russia from 1598 to 1605.
A protégé of Colonel Arana, this far-right military officer seized power in a 1954 coup to become the 28th president of Guatemala — who is it?
Carlos Castillo Armas: President of Guatemala from 1954 to 1957.

This American fleet admiral commanded the U.S. Pacific Fleet in World War II and, as the Navy's top submarine authority, helped push through approval for the first nuclear-powered submarine — who is he?
Chester W. Nimitz: American naval officer (1885–1966)
This Cold War-era proxy conflict broke out after a Central African nation's abrupt 1960 independence from Belgium, ending with Joseph-Désiré Mobutu in full control — which crisis?
Congo Crisis: 1960–1965 political unrest in Central Africa.
Claiming his predecessor was an imposter named Gaumata, this third King of Kings ruled the Achaemenid Empire at its territorial peak from 522 BCE — who was he?
Darius the Great: Persian ruler from 522 to 486 BCE.
Also known as Bacchus, this Greek god of wine, theatre, and ecstatic ritual madness carried a fennel-stem staff wound with ivy called a thyrsus — who is he?
Dionysus: Ancient Greek god of winemaking and wine.
Serving as the Soviet Union's last foreign minister from 1985 to 1991, this politician later led Georgia through multiple terms until resigning in 2003 — who is he?
Eduard Shevardnadze: Georgian politician and diplomat (1928–2014)
This term describes 18th-century European monarchs who wielded absolute power while claiming to rule for their subjects' well-being, inspired by Enlightenment ideas — what's it called?
Rising in early-20th-century Europe, which far-right ideology champions a dictatorial leader, militarism, and a belief in natural social hierarchy, in opposition to communism and democracy?
Son of a New Hampshire governor, this 14th president alienated anti-slavery groups by signing the Kansas-Nebraska Act and enforcing the Fugitive Slave Act. Who was he?
Franklin Pierce: President of the United States from 1853 to 1857.
Appointed by Stalin to lead the Soviet secret police from 1934 to 1936, this official oversaw the show trials of the Great Purge before becoming a victim of the very system he built — who is he?
Genrikh Yagoda: Soviet secret police official (1891–1938)
Founded in 918 and ruling until the rise of Joseon in 1392, this Korean dynasty unified the Later Three Kingdoms and gave its name to the modern word 'Korea' — what was it called?
Goryeo: Korean dynasty (918–1392). Throughout its existence, Goryeo, alongside Unified Silla, was known to be the Golden Age of Buddhism in Korea.
After 13 years running his country's intelligence service, this man became Turkey's Foreign Minister in 2023 and is widely seen as a possible successor to Erdoğan. Who is he?

In faiths with a linear history this afterlife place can be eternal, while reincarnation-based religions treat it as merely a stop between lives — and it's often imagined beneath the Earth's surface; what is it?
Hell: Abode of the dead, in various cultures.
Legend holds this samurai general never took a single wound across 57 military campaigns serving Tokugawa Ieyasu — which of the 'Four Heavenly Kings' is it?
Honda Tadakatsu: 16th-Century AD Japanese samurai, general and daimyo.

A Zaghawa commander who helped win the "Toyota War," he was purged and exiled to Libya, then stormed back to seize power — and ruled Chad for 30 years until he was killed during a 2021 offensive. Who was this longest-serving Chadian president?
Idriss Déby: President of Chad from 1990 to 2021.

Fought between the Kingdom of Italy and the Ottoman Empire from 1911 to 1912, this conflict ended with Italy gaining Libya per the Treaty of Ouchy, after Italian troops also seized the Dodecanese islands — which conflict was it?
Muslim conquest of the Iberian Peninsula
Italo-Turkish War: 1911–1912 war in Libya and the Aegean Sea.
A Polish politician known by his initials, he served in the European Parliament and led several parties before founding a new one in 2024 — who is he?
Janusz Korwin-Mikke: Polish far-right politician and publicist (born 1942)

After co-founding a coal brokerage company, this West Virginia politician served as governor before spending 15 years in the U.S. Senate, ultimately leaving the Democratic Party to become an independent in 2024 — who is he?
Joe Manchin: American politician and businessman (born 1947)
Identified by three Gospels as a member of the Sanhedrin, this biblical figure took responsibility for burying Jesus following the crucifixion — who was he?
Joseph of Arimathea: Biblical figure responsible for Jesus's burial.

As the 35th White House press secretary, this spokesperson became the first Black person and the first openly LGBTQ person to hold the role, having previously served as chief of staff for Kamala Harris's 2020 vice-presidential campaign — who is she?
Established in 1832 after the War of Independence, this monarchy survived on and off — including a 1935 restoration — until its final abolition in 1973. What was this Hellenic state called?
Kingdom of Greece: Period of Greek statehood from 1832 to 1923 and 1935 to 1973.

After the Moscow Armistice forced Finland to break ties with Germany in September 1944, fighting broke out in Finland's northernmost region as German troops withdrew toward occupied Norway — what's this conflict called?
Lapland War: 1944–1945 war between Finland and Germany.
Fought from 1558 to 1583 over present-day Estonia and Latvia, this conflict pitted Russia against a shifting coalition of Sweden, Denmark-Norway, and Poland-Lithuania — which conflict?
Livonian War: 16th-century war in Eastern Europe.
Born Sarah Breedlove, she built a fortune selling hair-care products for Black women and is recorded by Guinness as America's first female self-made millionaire — who was she?
Madam C. J. Walker: Black entrepreneur, philanthropist, and activist (1867–1919)
A Scottish heiress and socialite, this aristocrat became infamous for her scandalous, much-publicised 1963 divorce from her second husband — who was she?
Margaret Campbell, Duchess of Argyll: British socialite (1912–1993)
Nicknamed "The Flying Finn," this ski jumper won four Olympic golds — three of them at a single 1988 Games — making him one of the sport's greatest ever. Who was he?
Before becoming the 48th U.S. vice president, this Indiana Republican governed the state — and lost two House bids before working years as a conservative talk-show host. Who is he?
Mike Pence: Vice President of the United States from 2017 to 2021.

Reigning as Rama IV of the Chakri dynasty from 1851 to 1868, this Siamese king embraced Western science and technology, earning a posthumous title as his country's 'Father' of those fields — who was he?
Mongkut: King of Siam from 1851 to 1868. Mongkut (18 October 1804 – 1 October 1868), posthumously honoured as King Mongkut the Great was the king of Siam from the Chakri dynasty, titled Rama IV.

Chief minister of his state for 13 years, this politician rose to become India's prime minister in 2014 and is now India's longest-serving PM outside the Indian National Congress. He was introduced to a paramilitary organization at age eight. Who is he?
Narendra Modi: Prime Minister of India since 2014. Narendra Damodardas Modi (born 17 September 1950) is an Indian politician who has served as the prime minister of India since 26 May 2014.
Commanded by God to build an ark ahead of a great flood, this biblical patriarch later became the first person to cultivate a vineyard — who is he?
Noah: Biblical prophet known for building an ark.
This legendary Thracian musician could charm even stones with his lyre, sailed with Jason in search of the Golden Fleece, and journeyed into the underworld to reclaim his dead wife — who is he?
Orpheus: Legendary musician, poet, and prophet in Greek mythology.
This Finnish Green League politician served as Foreign Minister from 2019 to 2023 and became the first openly gay candidate to run for his country's presidency — who is he?
Once married to a future Roman emperor, this woman went on to become Nero's second wife, and a lavish excavated villa near Pompeii bears her name — who is she?
Poppaea Sabina: Roman empress from 62 to 65 AD.
A trained psychiatrist who became the first president of Republika Srpska, he spent twelve years as a fugitive before being convicted of genocide by a UN tribunal — who is he?
Radovan Karadžić: Bosnian Serb politician and war criminal (born 1945)
Designated Crown Prince during his father's 1967 coronation, this dissident has lived in exile in the US since the 1979 revolution that abolished the monarchy his family once ruled — who is he?
Reza Pahlavi: Former Crown Prince of Iran (born 1960)
A British peeress and former model who once worked as a political staffer, she is married to the 7th Marquess of Cholmondeley — who is she?
Grand Duchess Tatiana Nikolaevna of Russia
Rose Hanbury: English peeress and model (born 1984)

This Indian Army major with the National Security Guard's elite commando unit was killed in action during the 2008 Mumbai attacks and posthumously received India's highest peacetime gallantry award — who was he?

Once a member of the State Duma, this Russian financial fraudster's donation-based scheme defrauded thousands of investors — and he later claimed the same scheme was behind a bitcoin price rally — who is he?
Ending on the Fourth of July, 1863, this brutal Mississippi River campaign saw Grant trap Pemberton's Confederates in a fortress city — completing the Anaconda Plan's grip on the river. What was it?
Siege of Vicksburg: Battle of the American Civil War.

He out-debated and beat Abraham Lincoln for an 1858 Senate seat, then lost to him for the presidency two years later — and helped broker the Compromise of 1850 along the way. Which Illinois Democrat was he?
Stephen A. Douglas: American politician and lawyer (1813–1861)
A teacher, Marxist, and philosopher honored as a "Father of the Republic of Indonesia," this independence fighter founded the Murba Party and lived the life of a guerrilla and spy — who was he?
Tan Malaka: Indonesian communist philosopher, activist, and national hero (1897–1949)
Rising from Henry VIII's almoner to Lord Chancellor, this English cardinal controlled nearly every matter of state and held the Archbishopric of York — until his fall from royal favor. Who was he?
Thomas Wolsey: English statesman and cardinal (1473–1530)
Serving as ealdorman of Northumbria from 1006 until his assassination in 1016, this ruler's death sparked a blood feud with Thurbrand the Hold — who was he?
This Hungarian lawyer-politician has led the Fidesz party and served as prime minister twice, taking the country into NATO during his first stint. Who is he?
Viktor Orbán: Prime Minister of Hungary (1998–2002, 2010–2026)
This early American writer gave us 'Rip Van Winkle' and 'The Legend of Sleepy Hollow,' and later served as the U.S. ambassador to Spain — who was he?
Washington Irving: American writer, historian and diplomat (1783–1859)
Fought between 1939 and 1945, this global conflict remains history's deadliest, claiming 60 to 75 million lives and ending with the only nuclear weapons ever used in war — which conflict?
World War II: 1939–1945 global conflict. World War II, or the Second World War (1 September 1939 – 2 September 1945), was a global conflict between two coalitions: the Allies and the Axis powers.
Revered as the Father of the Nation, this ruler of Abu Dhabi became the first president of a newly unified Gulf federation in 1971?
Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan: President of the United Arab Emirates from 1971 to 2004.
Which of these four is the eldest?
Mikhail Lomonosov (born 1711) is the earliest of the four. One of the founders of modern geology, Lomonosov was also a poet and influenced the formation of the modern Russian literary language.
Which one below was born first?
Ellen Swallow Richards (born 1842) is the earliest of the four. Richards graduated from Westford Academy (second oldest secondary school in Massachusetts) in 1862.
Which of these four has been around longest?
R (programming language) (founded 1993) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four appeared earliest?
SQL (published 1986) is the earliest of the four.
Pick the physicist from these four.
Laura Bassi is a physicist. Laura Maria Caterina Bassi Veratti (29 October 1711 – 20 February 1778) was an Italian physicist and academic.
Pick the chemist from these four.
Antoine Lavoisier is a chemist. It is generally accepted that Lavoisier's great accomplishments in chemistry stem largely from his changing the science from a qualitative to a quantitative one.
What is the atomic number of Nitrogen?
Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
In what year was Richard Feynman born?
Richard Feynman: Richard Phillips Feynman (May 11, 1918 – February 15, 1988) was an American theoretical physicist.
In what year was Special relativity discovered?
Special relativity: In physics, the special theory of relativity, or simply special relativity, is a scientific theory of the relationship between space and time.
In what year was Mustard gas discovered?
Mustard gas: There is no preventive agent against mustard gas, with protection depending entirely on skin and airways protection, and no antidote exists for mustard poisoning.
Sodium acetate: Pfizer. Sodium acetate is a chemical compound with formula CH3COONa, also abbreviated NaOAc.
Which country is Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider from?

Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider: United States. Part of the Long Range Strike Bomber (LRS-B) program, it is to be an intercontinental strategic bomber that can deliver conventional and thermonuclear weapons.
Who is credited with discovering Archaea?
Archaea: Carl Woese. Archaea (ar-KEE-ə) is a domain of organisms.
Who is credited with discovering Synapse?
Synapse: Charles Scott Sherrington. In the nervous system, a synapse is a structure that allows a neuron to exchange (receive or send) signals with another cell in its immediate vicinity.
Who is credited with discovering Nitrogen?
Nitrogen: Daniel Rutherford. Nitrogen is a chemical element; it has symbol N and atomic number 7.
Known by the abbreviation NAC, this mucolytic drug treats acetaminophen overdose and also loosens thick mucus in people with chronic lung conditions like pneumonia and bronchitis — which drug?

Acetylcysteine (NAC) is a mucolytic that is used to treat paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose and to loosen thick mucus in individuals with chronic bronchopulmonary disorders, such as pneumonia and bronchitis.

Native to South America but cultivated in Europe since the 17th century for its fragrant oil, this flowering member of the verbena family is better known by a common name referencing a citrus fruit — what's its scientific name?
Aloysia citrodora is a species of flowering plant in the verbena family Verbenaceae, native to South America.
Whether contracted through the skin, the lungs, or the gut, this Bacillus-driven infection can take up to two months to show symptoms — what is it?
Anthrax is an infection caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis or Bacillus cereus biovar anthracis.
This common long-term inflammatory airway disease causes wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath that can flare into sudden attacks triggered by allergens or pollen. What condition is it?
Asthma is a common long-term inflammatory disease of the airways. It is characterized by variable and recurring symptoms and reduced lung function.

This fluid-dynamics rule holds that a fluid's pressure drops as its speed increases; the Swiss physicist credited with it published the idea in 1738, though Leonhard Euler derived the actual equation — what's it called?
Bernoulli's principle is a key concept in fluid dynamics that relates pressure, speed and height.
Native to South American tropical forests, this thorny ornamental vine, bush, or tree produces large colorful bracts surrounding three small waxy flowers — what is this plant genus?
Bougainvillea (US also BOH-) is a genus of thorny ornamental vines, bushes, and trees belonging to the family Nyctaginaceae.
Originating from the now-discredited caloric theory of heat, this unit of energy is defined as the amount of heat needed to raise one milliliter of water by one degree Celsius — name the unit?
Calorie is a unit of energy that originated from the caloric theory of heat.
Discovered in 1801 by Giuseppe Piazzi and initially hailed as a new planet, this object in the main asteroid belt is now the only recognized dwarf planet orbiting within Neptune's path — what is it?
Ceres (dwarf planet) is a dwarf planet in the main asteroid belt between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter.
After serving as dean of Harvard's Faculty of Arts and Sciences, this political scientist became the university's 30th president in July 2023 — who is she?
Claudine Gay (born August 4, 1970) is an American political scientist who is the Wilbur A. Cowett Professor of Government and of African and African-American Studies at Harvard University.
This transparent dome covering the iris and pupil provides about two-thirds of the eye's total focusing power and can be reshaped via LASIK surgery — what is it?
Cornea is the transparent front part of the eye which covers the iris, pupil, and anterior chamber.

Known by names ranging from the clinical to the crude to the childish — 'number two', 'dropping a deuce', 'doo-doo' — this basic biological process expels solid waste from the digestive tract. Name the process?

Defecation (or defaecation) follows digestion and is the necessary biological process by which organisms eliminate a solid, semisolid, or liquid waste material known as feces (or faeces) from the digestive tract via the anus or cloaca.
Best known for a single spiky, strong-smelling fruit beloved across Southeast Asia, this plant genus also includes eight other species with edible fruit — which genus?
Durio is a genus of plants in the family Malvaceae.

This broad set of measures — taken by individuals, advocacy groups, and governments alike — aims to prevent pollution, conserve natural resources, and maintain ecological balance, sometimes repairing existing damage — what is it called?
Environmental protection refers to the taking of measures to protecting the natural environment, prevent pollution and maintain ecological balance.
A legume plant from the family Fabaceae, its leaves and seeds have been common in dishes from the Indian subcontinent since ancient times — what is it?
Fenugreek (Trigonella foenum-graecum) is an annual plant in the family Fabaceae, with leaves consisting of three small obovate to oblong leaflets.
Its name comes from Greek for 'milk flower,' and this small genus of about 20 bulbous perennials nods with a single white bell of six tepals — what is the botanical name for the snowdrop?
Galanthus (from Ancient Greek, (gla, "milk") + (nthos, "flower")), or snowdrop, is a small genus of approximately 20 species of bulbous perennial herbaceous plants in the family Amaryllidaceae.
The largest living primate, with arm spans reaching 2.6 metres, this equatorial-African great ape shares up to 99% of its DNA with humans — what is it?
Gorilla are large, primarily herbivorous, great apes that live in the tropical forests of equatorial Africa.

Linked to conditions like tuberculosis, bronchitis, and lung cancer, this medical term describes blood discharged from the airway rather than internal bleeding elsewhere in the body. What is it called?
Hemoptysis is the discharge of blood or blood-stained mucus through the mouth coming from the bronchi, larynx, trachea, or lungs.
This negatively charged ion, one oxygen bonded to one hydrogen, acts as a base and forms industrially vital salts like the sodium version used to make millions of tons of chemicals. What ion is it?
Hydroxide (occasionally hydroxyl ion) is a diatomic anion with chemical formula OH.
One of the largest dog breeds in the world, this sighthound was historically used to course game and became the official mascot of a British Guards regiment in 1902. What breed is it?
Irish Wolfhound is a breed of large sighthound that has, by its presence and substantial size, inspired literature, poetry and mythology.
Originally trained as a mathematician, this English economist built the foundation for an entire school of macroeconomic thought that bears his name — who is he?

John Maynard Keynes (KAYNZ; 5 June 1883 - 21 April 1946), was an English economist whose writings are considered the basis for the school of thought known as Keynesian economics, as well as its various offshoots.
This fatal prion disease, once common among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea, was nicknamed 'laughing sickness' and spread through ritual funerary cannibalism. What is it?
Kuru (disease) was a rare, incurable, and fatal neurodegenerative disorder that was formerly common among the Fore people of Papua New Guinea.

This Finnish-American software engineer has led development of a hugely popular open-source operating system kernel since 1991, and also created the distributed version-control system Git — who is he?
Linus Torvalds (born 28 December 1969) is a Finnish and American software engineer who is the creator and lead developer of the Linux kernel since 1991.
This naturally occurring white solid, found as the mineral brucite, has very low water solubility and is a key ingredient in a well-known antacid remedy — what is it?
Magnesium hydroxide is an inorganic compound with the chemical formula Mg(OH)2.
Shaped like a half-moon, this crescent of fibrocartilage partly divides the knee joint and also turns up in the wrist, jaw, and shoulder joints — what is it called?
Meniscus (anatomy) (pl.: menisci or meniscuses) is a crescent-shaped fibrocartilaginous anatomical structure that, in contrast to an articular disc, only partly divides a joint cavity.
With over 86,000 living species spanning sea, freshwater, and even land, this is the largest of all marine phyla — what is it?
Mollusca is a phylum of protostomic invertebrate animals, whose members are known as molluscs or mollusks.

The first recognized fossil of this archaic human group was unearthed in 1856 in a German valley, and the species vanished around 40,000 years ago as modern humans arrived; who were these Pleistocene Europeans?

Neanderthal (nee-(r)-TAHL, nay-, -THAHL; Homo neanderthalensis or sometimes Homo sapiens neanderthalensis) are an extinct group of archaic humans who inhabited Europe and Western and Central Asia during the Middle to Late Pleistocene.
This insect order includes dragonflies and damselflies, the bulkier ones holding wings out at rest while the slender ones fold theirs along the body — what is it?
Odonata is an order of predatory flying insects that includes the dragonflies and damselflies (as well as the Epiophlebia damsel-dragonflies).
Usually numbering four and tucked behind the thyroid, these small endocrine structures release a hormone that kicks in when blood calcium runs low — which structures?
Parathyroid gland are small endocrine glands in the neck of humans and other tetrapods.
What dissociative anesthetic, known on the street as a recreational drug, can cause hallucinations, paranoia, and psychotic behavior, and is often smoked or mixed with cannabis or tobacco?
Phencyclidine (PCP), also known in its use as a street drug as angel dust among other names, is a dissociative anesthetic mainly used recreationally for its significant mind-altering effects.
Named after the American diplomat who introduced it to the US in the 1820s, this red-and-green plant native to Mexico is a Christmas staple — what plant is it?
Poinsettia (Euphorbia pulcherrima) is a commercially important flowering plant species of the diverse spurge family Euphorbiaceae.
This Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacterium selectively blocks antibiotics from crossing its outer membrane, making it a notorious cause of hospital-acquired pneumonia — what is it?
Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a common encapsulated, Gram-negative, aerobic-facultatively anaerobic, rod-shaped bacterium that can cause disease in plants and animals, including humans.

Almost exclusively affecting girls and emerging between 6 and 18 months of age, this genetic disorder, caused mainly by mutations in the MECP2 gene, brings repetitive movements, slowed growth, and language impairment — which condition?
Rett syndrome (RTT) is a genetic disorder that typically becomes apparent after 6-18 months of age and almost exclusively in girls.
Named for the Latin word for willow tree, from which it was first derived, this plant hormone is both a precursor to aspirin and a common ingredient in anti-acne skincare — which compound?
Salicylic acid is an organic compound with the formula C7H6O3.
Domesticated well over 3,000 years ago and grown widely in India, Myanmar, and Sudan today, this plant is considered one of the oldest oilseed crops known to humanity — what is it?
Sesame (Sesamum indicum) is a plant in the genus Sesamum, also called benne.
This use of the human voice for language ranges from informing and persuading to simply asking or declaring, combining vowels and consonants into meaningful words — what is it called?
Speech is the use of the human voice as a medium for language.
Among the most experienced spacewalkers in history, this NASA astronaut logged over 62 hours across nine spacewalks — the most of any woman — who is she?
Sunita Williams (ne Pandya; born September 19, 1965) is a retired United States Navy captain and former NASA astronaut.

Governed by four fundamental laws relating heat, work and temperature to energy and entropy, this branch of physics underpins chemical, mechanical and biochemical engineering alike — which field of physics?
Thermodynamics is a branch of physics that deals with heat, work, and temperature, and their relation to energy, entropy, and the physical properties of matter and radiation.
One of the earliest arthropod groups ever to appear in the fossil record, this extinct marine creature persisted in the oceans for nearly 270 million years across over 22,000 species — what is it?
Trilobite (meaning "three-lobed entities") are extinct marine arthropods that form the class Trilobita.

First described by John Edward Gray in 1821, this family of small feliform mammals spans Africa, southern Europe, and Asia on both sides of the Wallace Line, and includes the genets — name the family?
Viverridae is a family of small to medium-sized feliform mammals, comprising 14 genera with 33 species.
This Russian political activist and economist, described as the 'first lady' of her country's opposition, vowed to continue her late husband's work after fleeing into exile. Who is she?
Yulia Navalnaya (ne Abrosimova; born 24 July 1976) is a Russian political activist and economist.

A key figure of the Scottish Enlightenment, this philosopher wrote The Theory of Moral Sentiments before the 1776 work often called the inception of modern economics — who is the "father of economics"?
Adam Smith: Scottish economist and philosopher (1723–1790)
Belonging to the birch family and found throughout the north temperate zone, this genus of about 35 tree and shrub species even reaches into the Andes — what genus is it?
Alder: Genus of flowering plants in the birch family Betulaceae.
Sold under the brand name Norvasc, this long-acting calcium channel blocker treats high blood pressure and variant angina by relaxing and widening the arteries — what's the drug?
Amlodipine: Medication against high blood pressure.
Born Fernando Martins de Bulhões, this 13th-century Portuguese Catholic priest joined the Order of Friars Minor — who is he?
Anthony of Padua: Portuguese Catholic saint (1195–1231)
This Russian designer and outspoken blogger, known for provocative and often obscene commentary, founded a namesake design studio and is a descendant of the Tolstoy family — who is he?
Artemy Lebedev: Russian designer and businessman (born 1975)
Sold as Zithromax, this antibiotic tackles strep throat, pneumonia and traveler's diarrhea — but its tendency to cause QT prolongation keeps doctors watchful of the heart. Which drug is it?
Azithromycin: Antibiotic. It is administered by mouth, into a vein, or as topical treatment for the eye.
A likely hybrid of lemon and a bitter citrus relative, this fragrant fruit flavors tea, snus, and perfume, though it can heighten skin's sensitivity to sunlight — which fruit?
Credited with kicking off the Jet Age, this swept-wing quadjet airliner entered regular passenger service with Pan Am in October 1958 — which aircraft?

Best known for his role as Ben Hunter in a soapy prime-time revenge drama, this American actor also starred as Will Davis on The CW's 'Privileged' and Kyle Parks on Lifetime's 'The Client List.' Who is he?
Its dihydrate form is the mineral gypsum and its dehydrated cousin is bassanite; sparingly soluble, it causes permanent hardness in water — which inorganic salt is this?
Calcium sulfate: Chemical derived from gypsum used in food and industry.
A nerve compression syndrome caused when the median nerve in the wrist becomes compressed, causing numbness and tingling in the thumb and fingers. What is this condition?
Carpal tunnel syndrome: Compression of the median nerve in the wrist. It can also be measured with electrodiagnostic tests.
Also known as silver beet or perpetual spinach, this leafy green shares its species with beetroot — which vegetable?
Chard: Green leafy vegetable. Chard (Beta vulgaris subsp. vulgaris, Cicla Group and Flavescens Group) is a green leafy vegetable.
Sold under the brand name Celexa, this SSRI antidepressant treats major depressive disorder, OCD, panic disorder, and social anxiety — what is it?
Citalopram: SSRI antidepressant. Citalopram, sold under the brand name Celexa among others, is an antidepressant of the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) class.
This icy wanderer of the solar system grows a gassy halo and sometimes a tail stretching more than an astronomical unit as it nears the sun — what is it?
Comet: Natural object in space that releases gas.
Smelling of vanilla but tasting bitter, which plant compound isn't itself an anticoagulant, though its derivatives inspired the blood-thinning drug warfarin?
This Zambian-born economist turned heads with four New York Times bestsellers, including "Dead Aid," which argues that foreign aid actually holds Africa back. Which author and life peer is it?
Dambisa Moyo, Baroness Moyo: Zambian-born economist (born February 1969)
Known for feigning death when cornered, which genus of cat-sized marsupials includes the only marsupial species found north of Mexico?
Didelphis: Genus of marsupials. The six species in the genus Didelphis, commonly known as Large American opossums, are members of the opossum order, Didelphimorphia.
Nicknamed 'Viking disease,' this hand condition — first surgically treated in 1831 by the surgeon it's named after — permanently curls the ring finger inward. What is it?
Dupuytren's contracture: Medical condition featuring permanent bending of fingers.
A Swedish scientist and inventor until, at 53, dreams and visions sent him into a spiritual phase, this polymath became best known for his 1758 book on the afterlife, Heaven and Hell — who was he?
Emanuel Swedenborg: Swedish scientist, philosopher, and theologian (1688–1772)
With a sweet smell like pear drops, this colorless solvent turns up in nail-polish remover and is used to decaffeinate tea and coffee. What is it?
Named after a 19th-century English physicist, this SI unit measures a material's ability to store electrical charge, equal to one coulomb per volt — what is it?
Farad: SI unit of electric capacitance.
Originally focused on water, this branch of physics studies liquids, gases, and plasmas, with applications from geophysics to aerospace engineering — which field?
Fluid mechanics: Branch of physics. Fluid mechanics is the branch of physics concerned with the mechanics of fluids (liquids, gases, and plasmas) and the forces on them.
Bound together by gravity, this vast system of stars, gas, dust, and dark matter can range from a dwarf with under a thousand stars to a supergiant with a hundred trillion — what is it?
Galaxy: System of stars and interstellar matter. The word is derived from the Greek galaxias (γαλαξίας), meaning 'milky', a reference to the Milky Way galaxy that contains the Solar System.
The last survivor of an order that first appeared over 290 million years ago, this long-lived East Asian tree with unique fan-shaped leaves is celebrated as a living fossil — what is it?
Ginkgo biloba: Species of tree. Fossils similar to the living species, belonging to the genus Ginkgo, extend back to the Middle Jurassic epoch about 170 million years ago.

After proving a 20-year-old open problem in Riemannian geometry known as the soul conjecture, this reclusive Russian mathematician later quit the field entirely and now lives in seclusion in Saint Petersburg — who is he?

In 2018 this Chinese biophysicist announced the world's first gene-edited human babies — twin girls modified for HIV resistance — which got him onto Time's influential list and fired from his university. Who was he?
This branch of biology studies the microscopic structure of tissues, historically distinguished from cytology (the study of cells) and organology (the study of organs) — what is it called?
Histology: Study of the microscopic anatomy of cells and tissues of plants and animals.
A yellow-flowered perennial whose leaves look perforated by translucent glands, this plant is famed in folklore and traditional medicine under a saintly common name — what is its botanical name?
Hypericum perforatum: Flowering plant in the St John's wort family.
Endemic to semiarid central-eastern Australia and also called the "fierce snake," this elapid was rediscovered in 1972 after nearly 90 years of obscurity — what is it?
Inland taipan: Extremely venomous snake native to Australia.

This Dutch microscopist showed that an insect's egg, larva, pupa, and adult are all one animal, pioneered the microscope in dissections, and in 1658 became the first to observe red blood cells — who was he?
Jan Swammerdam: Dutch biologist and microscopist (1637–1680)
Equal to the work done when a one-newton force moves an object one metre, this SI unit of energy is named for a 19th-century English physicist — which unit?
Joule: SI unit of energy. The joule ( JOOL, or JOWL; symbol: J) is the unit of energy in the International System of Units (SI).
Living as a recluse in a log house outside Kaluga, this Russian pioneer of rocket science inspired both Wernher von Braun and the architects of the Soviet space program — who is he?
Distinguished by coloured scales, large triangular wings, and a nectar-sipping proboscis, which insect order encompasses both butterflies and moths?
Lepidoptera: Order of insects including moths and butterflies.
Based on the L-188 Electra airliner and distinguished by a tail 'stinger' used to magnetically detect submarines, this four-engine turboprop has served the US Navy since the 1960s — which aircraft?
Lockheed P-3 Orion: Maritime patrol and anti-submarine aircraft family.
Known historically as 'magnesia alba' to distinguish it from a manganese-containing mineral called 'magnesia nigra,' this white hygroscopic solid has the formula MgO — what is it?
Magnesium oxide: Chemical compound naturally occurring as periclase.
Awarded a share of the 1954 Nobel Prize in Physics for his statistical interpretation of the wavefunction, this Göttingen-trained theorist helped found quantum mechanics — who is he?
First isolated in 1921 and encoded by the codon AUG, this essential amino acid also serves as the precursor to cysteine — which amino acid is this?
Nicknamed the 'powerhouse of the cell' after a phrase popularized in a 1957 magazine article, this double-membraned organelle generates ATP through respiration — which organelle?
Mitochondrion: Organelle in eukaryotic cells responsible for respiration.
Despite its name, this blister-agent chemical weapon isn't always gaseous, and to this day there is no antidote for exposure to it — what is it?
Mustard gas: Chemical warfare agent. There is no preventive agent against mustard gas, with protection depending entirely on skin and airways protection, and no antidote exists for mustard poisoning.
This medical specialty diagnoses and treats disorders of the brain, spinal cord, and peripheral nerves, from epilepsy and stroke to Parkinson's disease — which field?
Neurology: Medical specialty dealing with disorders of the nervous system.

Producing a distinctive capped nut and supporting more than 950 species of caterpillar, this keystone hardwood genus ranges across the Northern Hemisphere in some 500 species, some evergreen, some deciduous — what tree is it?
Oak: Tree or shrub in the genus Quercus.
A playful, fish-eating cousin of weasels and badgers, this semiaquatic mammal is known for sliding down natural slides and toying with stones — what is it?
A Scottish biologist-turned-town-planner, he coined the word 'conurbation' and gave us one of the earliest versions of 'think globally, act locally' in social science — who was he?
Patrick Geddes: Scottish scientist and town planner (1854–1932)
Known on the street as 'angel dust,' this dissociative anesthetic acts as an NMDA receptor antagonist and can cause hallucinations and psychosis — what is this drug?
Phencyclidine: Dissociative hallucinogenic drug, mostly used recreationally.
Native to Eurasia and temperate Africa but now naturalized worldwide, this flowering plant shares a common name with a banana-like fruit despite being unrelated to it — which species?
Plantago major: Species of flowering plant in the plantain family Plantaginaceae.
Covering the front part of the frontal lobe, this brain region orchestrates higher-order thinking including focus, decision-making, and impulse control — what is it?
Prefrontal cortex: Part of the brain responsible for personality, decision-making, and social behavior.
Named by the medieval scholar Gerard of Cremona, this black-looking opening in the eye's iris is round in humans but a vertical slit in cats and a horizontal bar in goats — what is it?
Pupil: Part of an eye. The pupil is a hole located in the center of the iris of the eye that allows light to strike the retina.
Native to western Europe and known scientifically as Ribes rubrum, which widely cultivated berry has escaped into the wild across many regions?
Redcurrant: Flowering plant species in the family Grossulariaceae.

He dreamed up an "impossible" triangle, traded ideas with M. C. Escher, and shared the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for proving black holes are a robust prediction of general relativity — who is this English mathematician?
Roger Penrose: English mathematician, mathematical physicist (born 1931)
A pharmaceutical chemist with a Dartmouth Ph.D. by day, this American has chaired Anthrocon — one of the world's largest furry conventions — since 1999. Who is he?
Samuel Conway: American chemist and furry fandom personality.
Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754, this term for a lucky accidental discovery describes how penicillin, Post-it Notes, and the microwave oven all came about — what is it?
Lose your coiled shell entirely and you're called a slug; keep one big enough to retract into and you're this shelled gastropod instead — what creature?
Snail: Shelled gastropod. The name is most often applied to land snails, terrestrial pulmonate gastropod molluscs.
This rodent family includes tree-dwelling, ground-dwelling, and gliding members like chipmunks and prairie dogs, and traces its fossil record back to the Eocene epoch — which animal family?
Squirrel: Family of rodents. The squirrel family includes tree squirrels, ground squirrels (including chipmunks and prairie dogs, among others), and flying squirrels.
Designed by R. J. Mitchell with a distinctive elliptical wing and sunken rivets for minimal drag, this was the only British fighter kept in continuous production throughout World War II — what is it?
Supermarine Spitfire: British single-seat WWII fighter aircraft.
Known as the barn funnel weaver in North America and simply the house spider in Europe, this species belongs to the funnel-web family Agelenidae — which arachnid?
Also called T4, this hormone produced by the thyroid gland acts as a precursor to the more active T3 and helps regulate metabolism, heart function and bone health — what is it?
Thyroxine: Thyroid hormone. It is the primary form of thyroid hormone found in the blood and acts as a prohormone of the more active thyroid hormone, triiodothyronine (T3).
This ester of glycerol and three fatty acids is the main constituent of body fat and a major component of human skin oils — what is it?
Triglyceride: Any ester of glycerol having all three hydroxyl groups esterified with fatty acids.

With co-researcher James Cronin, this American nuclear physicist won the 1980 Nobel for a 1964 K-meson experiment proving certain subatomic reactions aren't indifferent to time — discovering CP violation. Who was he?
Val Logsdon Fitch: American nuclear physicist. Born on a cattle ranch near Merriman, Nebraska, Fitch was drafted into the U.S.
Botanically a berry called a 'pepo,' this trailing vine's fruit comes in over 1,000 varieties and has a rind that's actually edible once cooked — what is it?
Black-and-yellow social wasps that live in colonies and do a rapid side-to-side wiggle just before landing go by what North American common name?
Yellowjacket: Common name for two genera of wasps.
The symbol for beryllium is Be. Beryllium is a chemical element; it has symbol Be and atomic number 4.
The symbol for palladium is Pd. Palladium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Pd and atomic number 46.
